newsitem.title: KENYA: Refugees cram into world's biggest camp in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Refugees cram into world's biggest camp in Zaire.

text.p: Aid workers sweated on Tuesday to dig latrines and avert disaster at the Mugunga camp in eastern Zaire which fugitives from war have turned into the world's biggest refugee camp, crammed with about 400,000 people.
Aid officials said the Rwandan Hutu refugees faced twin threats of disease and food shortages, as local supplies have been disrupted by fighting between Zairean troops and Tutsi rebels.
Fruit and vegetable supplies are dwindling and food prices in the region are skyrocketing, to the fury of local Zairean residents, they said.
"People are complaining today they cannot afford to buy bread any more," said spokesman Panos Moumtzis of the U.N. refugee agency (UNHCR) in the east Zaire city of Goma, close to the Mugunga camp.
"It is extremely worrying, a potential timebomb," he said of the general situation in the region, where scattered fighting continues.
Zaire announced on Monday night it was suspending all commercial air links to the troubled region to try to contain ethnic warfare.

A government spokesman in Kinshasa said President Mobutu Sese Seko, convalescing in Switzerland after a prostate cancer operation on August 22, had placed North and South Kivu provinces in the east under emergency rule.

"The situation in eastern Zaire is now desperate. UNHCR is cut off from all but 400,000 of the one million refugees in eastern Zaire," spokeswoman Ruth Marshall told a Geneva briefing at UNHCR headquarters.
She said food stocks in Goma region were enough for less than a week following the looting of a U.N. food warehouse at the weekend.
Marshall said the only refugees UNHCR had direct access to were in Lac Vert and Mugunga camps in Goma region where UNHCR started food distribution on Tuesday.

The U.N. aim is to try to avoid a replay of 1994, when thousands of Rwandan Hutu refugees died of cholera in stinking, overcrowded camps in eastern Zaire. They fled civil war in Rwanda and retribution for the anti-Tutsi genocide in which many refugees actively participated.
The same refugees were on the move again in past days as the Hutu-Tutsi conflict shifted dramatically onto Zairean soil.
After attacks at the weekend on the Kibumba camp next to the Rwandan border, about 200,000 Hutu Rwandans fled west to the existing Mugunga camp.
"The terrain is rock. You cannot put a nail down," said Moumtzis. "It is difficult to dig latrines and even put up shelters."
"If the rain starts there is a great risk of epidemics which is why we are increasing sanitation and water today. We have 40 latrine teams with five to 10 people in each digging latrines," he said.
Lots of refugees have bleeding feet, he said, after walking on rocky paths to reach the camp.
The UNHCR has appealed to the Hutu refugees to return home to Rwanda, but very few have heeded the call since they fear reprisals from the Tutsi minority now ruling the country.
U.N. officials say that over the last few days only 710 refugees returned to Rwanda from the Goma region, at the northern end of Lake Kivu, while 322 crossed at Cyangugu, at the lake's southern end.
